report:
**Conclusion: The evidence that whole-body vibration (WBV) therapy prevents fractures in osteoporosis sufferers is weak and inconclusive. Your sister's "yes" is not well supported.**

Most research on WBV focuses on surrogate outcomes like bone mineral density (BMD) and balance, not fractures themselves. A Cochrane protocol highlighted that whether WBV is effective for preventing/treating osteoporosis remained unproven, and reviewers noted claims "cannot be made without further research" (https://www.cochrane.org/CD008417/MUSKEL_whole-body-vibration-for-preventing-and-treating-osteoporosis). A 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis concluded WBV "may be clinically useful as non-pharmacological/adjunct therapy to mitigate osteoporosis risk in healthy postmenopausal females," but called for more studies on mechanisms—hardly a fracture-prevention endorsement (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0965229922000139).

Trials are inconsistent. One study found low-magnitude WBV significantly reduced lumbar spine bone loss and aided fall prevention (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4758089/), while another concluded low-magnitude WBV "is not an effective therapy for the prevention of bone loss in postmenopausal women" (https://medicalxpress.com/news/2011-11-popular-whole-body-vibration-effective-therapy-bone.html). A 2025 falls-prevention review rated WBV as "low certainty for benefit in reducing fractures."

No major osteoporosis guideline lists WBV as a fracture-preventing therapy, and vibrating platforms are not FDA-approved for medical purposes. WBV may modestly help BMD or balance in some groups, but current evidence does not establish that it prevents osteoporotic fractures.
